children.title: Pointed Polyhedra
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral sets without nontrivial lineality.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is pointed exactly when \(\operatorname{lin}(P)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard finite-dimensional pointedness convention for nonempty polyhedra.

source_refs.locator: 5. Geometry p. 20

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The polyhedron \(P\) is pointed if it contains no affine line. Explicitly, there do not exist \(x\in P\) and \(d\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\) such that
\[
\{x+td:t\in\mathbb R\}\subseteq P.
\]
Equivalently, \(P\) is pointed if and only if its lineality space is trivial:
\[
\operatorname{lin}(P)=\{0\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedron is pointed when it contains no line, equivalently when its lineality space contains only the zero direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointed Polyhedra

children.title: Nonpointed Polyhedra

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is nonpointed exactly when \(\operatorname{lin}(P)\neq\{0\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The polyhedron \(P\) is nonpointed if it contains an affine line. Thus there exist \(x\in P\) and \(d\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\) such that
\[
x+td\in P\qquad\text{for every }t\in\mathbb R.
\]
Equivalently, \(P\) is nonpointed if and only if
\[
\operatorname{lin}(P)\neq\{0\}.
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L=\operatorname{lin}(P)\). The pointedness regimes are separated exactly by
\[
L=\{0\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P\text{ is pointed},
\]
and
\[
L\neq\{0\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P\text{ is nonpointed}.
\]
For an inequality description \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\), this boundary is equivalently \(\ker A=\{0\}\) versus \(\ker A\neq\{0\}\), because \(L=\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact boundary is whether the lineality space is trivial: zero lineality means pointed, while any nonzero lineality means nonpointed.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty polyhedron with lineality space \(L\).
\(N\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-\dim L)}\) has columns forming a basis of \(L^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The projected polyhedron \(Q=N^{\mathsf T}P\) is pointed and satisfies \(P=NQ+L\).

notation.meaning: An orthonormal basis matrix for the orthogonal complement of L.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonal quotient reduction removing all lineality directions.

source_refs.locator: 5. Geometry p. 20

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose the columns of \(N\) orthonormally, so \(N^{\mathsf T}N=I\) and \(\operatorname{range}N=L^\perp\), and define
\[
Q=N^{\mathsf T}P=\{N^{\mathsf T}x:x\in P\}.
\]
Then \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-\dim L}\) is a pointed polyhedron. Moreover,
\[
P=NQ+L=\{Nz+\ell:z\in Q,\ \ell\in L\}.
\]
Thus projection onto \(L^\perp\), equivalently passage to the quotient \(\mathbb R^n/L\), removes precisely the lineality of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting a polyhedron orthogonally away from its lineality produces a pointed polyhedron, while the original set is recovered by adding the lineality space.
knowledge_statements.title: Line-Free Reductions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adjacent Basic Solutions and Edges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinct basic solutions of the same linear-constraint system in \(\mathbb R^n\); feasibility is additionally required for the edge clause.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x,y\in\mathbb R^n\) be distinct basic solutions of the same system of linear constraints. If the adjacent basic solutions \(x\) and \(y\) are also feasible, the line segment \([x,y]=\{(1-t)x+ty:0\le t\le1\}\) is called an edge of the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two distinct basic solutions in n-dimensional space are adjacent when they share n−1 linearly independent active constraints. If the adjacent solutions are feasible, the segment joining them is called an edge of the feasible set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Slack-form basic solutions and directions for linear-inequality systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines normal basic feasible solutions and basic feasible directions through slack extensions and records their finite and optimization consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\). A vector \(v\in\mathbb R^n\) is a normal basic feasible solution of \(Ax\le b\) when its slack extension \((v_1,\ldots,v_n,v_{n+1},\ldots,v_{n+m})\), with \(v_{n+i}=b_i-\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}v_j\), is a normal basic feasible solution of \(\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}x_j+x_{n+i}=b_i\), \(x_{n+i}\ge0\). A vector \(w\in\mathbb R^n\) is a basic feasible direction when its extension with \(w_{n+i}=-\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}w_j\) is a basic feasible direction of that slack system. Every system \(Ax\le b\) has finitely many normal basic feasible solutions and basic feasible directions, and every basic feasible direction satisfies \(Aw\le0\). If \(\max\{cx:Ax\le b\}\) has an optimal solution, some basic feasible solution is optimal; if it is unbounded above, some basic feasible direction \(w\) satisfies \(cw>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Basic solutions and directions of an inequality system are defined through its nonnegative-slack equality form. There are finitely many of each, every basic direction is a recession direction, an attained optimum has a basic optimum, and unboundedness has an improving basic direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\operatorname{NBFS}(P)|<\infty,\quad |\operatorname{BFD}(P)|<\infty,\quad \operatorname{BFD}(P)\subseteq\{w:Aw\le0\},\quad \operatorname{argmax}_{x\in P}cx\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow\exists\text{ a basic optimal solution},\quad \sup_{x\in P}cx=+\infty\Rightarrow\exists w\in\operatorname{BFD}(P):cw>0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic Feasible Partitions, Neighbors, and Closed Lists
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis-state encoding and adjacency definitions for bounded-variable basic feasible solutions whose free variables are basic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(Ax=b\), \(\ell\le x\le u\), and a basic feasible solution \(x^*\) in which every free variable is basic. Its basic feasible partition is the vector \(e\in\{0,1,2\}^n\) defined by \[e_k=\begin{cases}1,&x_k\text{ is basic},\\0,&x_k\text{ is nonbasic and }x_k^*=\ell_k<u_k,\\2,&x_k\text{ is nonbasic and }x_k^*=u_k.\end{cases}\] Two partitions are neighbors if one is obtained from the other by a single pivot exchanging one nonbasic and one basic variable, or by switching one nonbasic variable from one bound to the other while leaving the basis unchanged. A basic feasible direction is a neighbor of a partition when they have the same set of basic variables. A list of basic feasible partitions and basic feasible directions is closed if it contains every neighbor of each listed partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basic feasible partition records whether each variable is basic, nonbasic at its lower bound, or nonbasic at its upper bound. Neighboring partitions differ by one basis exchange or one nonbasic bound switch; a neighboring basic feasible direction uses the same basis. A list is closed when it includes every neighbor of each listed partition.
assumptions_latex: x^*\text{ is a basic feasible solution with every free variable basic}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: e_k=\begin{cases}1,&x_k\text{ basic},\\0,&x_k\text{ nonbasic at }\ell_k<u_k,\\2,&x_k\text{ nonbasic at }u_k,\end{cases}\quad\text{with adjacency and closure defined by single pivots, bound switches, and same-basis feasible directions.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp cardinality form of the active-constraint characterization in ambient dimension n.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^Tx\le b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\). Then \(x\) is a vertex of \(P\) if and only if \(x\in P\) and there exists \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) with \(|I|=n\) such that \(x\) is the unique solution of \(a_i^Ty=b_i\) for all \(i\in I\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Representation and Completeness of a Closed Basic-Partition List
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-conic representation and basis-enumeration completeness for a closed list containing at least one basic feasible partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\). Let \(e^1,\ldots,e^M,w^1,\ldots,w^N\) be a closed list of basic feasible partitions and basic feasible directions of this system, and let \(v^r\) be the basic feasible solution determined by \(e^r\). If \(M>0\), then \[x^*\in P\iff x^*=\sum_{r=1}^M p_rv^r+\sum_{s=1}^N q_sw^s\] for some \(p_r,q_s\ge0\) satisfying \(\sum_{r=1}^M p_r=1\). Moreover, every basic feasible solution of the system in which all free variables are basic is one of \(v^1,\ldots,v^M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a closed list contains at least one basic feasible partition, every feasible point is a convex combination of the listed basic feasible solutions plus a nonnegative combination of the listed directions. The list also contains every basic feasible solution in which all free variables are basic.
assumptions_latex: v^r\text{ is the basic feasible solution determined by }e^r
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\in P\iff\exists p\ge0,\ q\ge0:\ x^*=\sum_{r=1}^M p_rv^r+\sum_{s=1}^N q_sw^s,\ \sum_{r=1}^M p_r=1;\quad\text{every qualifying basic feasible solution lies in }\{v^1,\ldots,v^M\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic and basic feasible solutions with variable bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines bounded-variable basic solutions and partitions, feasibility, degeneracy, partition adjacency, and partition multiplicity at degenerate extreme points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have rank \(m\), and consider \(Ax=b\) with bounds \(\ell\le x\le u\). A solution \(\bar x\) of \(A\bar x=b\) is basic if \(A=[B,N_1,N_2]\), where \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) is nonsingular, \(\bar x_{N_1}=\ell_{N_1}\), \(\bar x_{N_2}=u_{N_2}\), and \(\bar x_B=B^{-1}(b-N_1\ell_{N_1}-N_2u_{N_2})\). It is basic feasible if \(\ell_B\le \bar x_B\le u_B\), nondegenerate if \(\ell_B<\bar x_B<u_B\), and degenerate otherwise. The corresponding column partition is a basic or basic feasible partition. Two such partitions are adjacent when all but one nonbasic variable coincide at the same bounds. At a degenerate extreme point, each choice of \(n-m\) binding bound hyperplanes that, together with the \(m\) equality constraints, forms \(n\) linearly independent binding hyperplanes determines an associated basic feasible partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a full-row-rank equality system, a bounded-variable basic solution fixes every nonbasic variable at a lower or upper bound and obtains the basic variables from a nonsingular basis. It is feasible when its basic variables satisfy their bounds and nondegenerate when they satisfy them strictly. Adjacent basic partitions agree on all but one bound-fixed nonbasic variable. A degenerate extreme point may correspond to multiple qualifying basic feasible partitions.
assumptions_latex: A=[B,N_1,N_2],\quad B\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\text{ is nonsingular}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\text{ is basic feasible}\iff \bar x_{N_1}=\ell_{N_1},\ \bar x_{N_2}=u_{N_2},\ \bar x_B=B^{-1}(b-N_1\ell_{N_1}-N_2u_{N_2}),\ \ell_B\le \bar x_B\le u_B.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Breadth-First Enumeration of Basic Feasible Partitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Procedure requiring an initial basic feasible partition and a means of producing all neighbors. The extract alone does not establish that every vertex or direction is reachable, nor that distinct partitions yield distinct solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(\mathbf e^1=\mathbf e^*\), \(M=1\), \(N=0\), and \(k=1\), and let \(\mathbf v^1\) be the basic feasible solution determined by \(\mathbf e^1\). Produce all neighbors of \(\mathbf e^k\). Append each basic feasible partition not already among \(\mathbf e^1,\ldots,\mathbf e^M\), together with its determined basic feasible solution, and append each basic feasible direction not already among \(\mathbf w^1,\ldots,\mathbf w^N\). If \(k=M\), stop; otherwise replace \(k\) by \(k+1\) and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from one basic feasible partition, process listed partitions in breadth-first order. Record every newly encountered neighboring basic feasible partition and its associated basic feasible solution, and separately record every newly encountered basic feasible direction. Stop after the last currently listed partition has been processed. This procedure alone does not prove global completeness.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbf e^*\) is a basic feasible partition.
All neighbors of each processed basic feasible partition can be produced.
Previously listed basic feasible partitions and directions can be recognized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Upon reaching \(k=M\), every basic feasible partition placed on the list has been processed, and the lists contain the distinct partitions and directions encountered during the traversal, together with the basic feasible solution associated with each listed partition.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a convex polyhedron and let \(u,v\in\operatorname{ext}(C)\) be distinct. The segment \(S=[u,v]\) is an edge of \(C\) if and only if no point \(z\in S\) is the midpoint of two points lying in \(C\setminus S\). When this condition holds, \(u\) and \(v\) are called neighbors or adjacent extreme points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertices and faces of a convex polyhedron
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines vertices by unique linear maximization and proper faces by supporting hyperplanes, with edges and vertices classified by dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be a convex polyhedron. A point v\in P is a vertex of P if there exists c\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\} such that c^Tv>c^Ty for every y\in P\setminus\{v\}. If \dim P=n, then F\subseteq P is a k-dimensional face when \dim F=k and there exist c\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\} and z\in\mathbb{R} such that c^Tx=z for every x\in F and c^Tx<z for every x\in P\setminus F. Such an F equals P\cap\{x:c^Tx=z\} and is a convex polyhedron. An edge is a one-dimensional face, and a vertex is a zero-dimensional face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex uniquely maximizes some nonconstant linear function over the polyhedron. For a full-dimensional polyhedron, a face is the set touched by a supporting hyperplane, with every other point strictly on one side. Faces are themselves polyhedra; edges are one-dimensional faces and vertices are zero-dimensional faces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v\text{ is a vertex under the unique-maximizer condition; }F\text{ is a }k\text{-dimensional face under the supporting-hyperplane condition; edges and vertices are respectively one- and zero-dimensional faces.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral faces, dimensions, facets, and adjacent vertices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Face taxonomy for a polyhedron in ambient dimension n.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A face \(F\) of a polyhedron \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is the set of points of \(X\) on which a nonempty collection of defining hyperplanes is active. If \(r(F)\) is the maximum number of linearly independent defining hyperplanes active at every point of \(F\), then \(\dim F=n-r(F)\). Thus vertices are zero-dimensional faces and edges are one-dimensional faces. Moreover, \(\dim X=n-r(X)\), and \(X\) is full-dimensional exactly when \(r(X)=0\). By the stated convention, \(X\) and \(\varnothing\) may be called improper faces and all other faces proper. If \(\dim X\ge1\), a facet is a proper face of dimension \(\dim X-1\). Two vertices are adjacent exactly when their joining segment is an edge; consequently they share \(n-1\) linearly independent active defining hyperplanes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face consists of the feasible points satisfying a nonempty collection of defining inequalities at equality. If r(F) is the largest number of independent defining hyperplanes active throughout F, its dimension is n minus r(F). Vertices and edges are respectively zero- and one-dimensional faces. The polyhedron is full-dimensional exactly when no independent defining hyperplane is active throughout it. Under the given convention, the polyhedron and the empty set are improper faces; the others are proper. A facet has dimension one below that of the polyhedron. Two vertices are adjacent exactly when their connecting segment is an edge, and they therefore share n minus one independent active hyperplanes.
assumptions_latex: r(F)=\max\{\text{number of linearly independent defining hyperplanes active throughout }F\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \dim F=n-r(F),\quad \dim X=n-r(X),\quad X\text{ full-dimensional}\iff r(X)=0;\quad \dim(\text{facet})=\dim X-1;\quad u,v\text{ adjacent}\iff [u,v]\text{ is an edge}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Two standard face families are
\[
\mathcal F_{+}(P)=\{F\subseteq P:F\neq\varnothing\text{ and }F\text{ is supported}\}
\]
and the augmented family
\[
\mathcal F(P)=\mathcal F_{+}(P)\cup\{\varnothing\}.
\]
Both include \(P\), usually called the improper face. knowledge_statements.title: Facets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative-dimension definition valid for non-full-dimensional polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The face \(F\) is a facet of \(P\) if it has codimension one relative to the affine hull of \(P\):
\[
\dim F=d-1,\qquad d=\dim P.
\]
Equivalently, \(F\) is a maximal proper face under inclusion: there is no face \(G\) satisfying \(F\subsetneq G\subsetneq P\). The dimension is relative, so full dimensionality of \(P\) in \(\mathbb R^n\) is not required.

\(F\) is a nonempty proper face of \(P\).

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Face Lattices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The inclusion lattice of all faces of a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a polyhedron \(P\), let \(\mathcal{F}(P)\) contain every face, including \(\varnothing\) and \(P\), ordered by inclusion. Then \(\mathcal{F}(P)\) is a finite lattice. For faces \(F,G\in\mathcal{F}(P)\), their meet is \(F\wedge G=F\cap G\), and their join is \[F\vee G=\bigcap\{H\in\mathcal{F}(P):F\cup G\subseteq H\},\] the smallest face containing both.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and define \(P=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^n:Au\le b\}\). For \(x\in P\), write the rows of \(A\) as \(a_i^{\mathsf T}\) and define \(I(x)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:a_i^{\mathsf T}x=b_i\}\). The following are equivalent: \(x\) is an extreme point of \(P\); \(\{x\}\) is a zero-dimensional face of \(P\); \(\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}\) spans \(\mathbb{R}^n\); \(x\) is the unique vector \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \(a_i^{\mathsf T}y=b_i\) for every \(i\in I(x)\); and the only \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \(A_{I(x)}d=0\) is \(d=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polyhedron, being an extreme point, having a singleton zero-dimensional face, having active normals that span the ambient space, being uniquely determined by the active equalities, and having a trivial active-constraint kernel are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ is extreme}\iff \{x\}\text{ is a zero-dimensional face of }P\iff \operatorname{span}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}=\mathbb{R}^n\iff x\text{ is uniquely determined by the active equalities}\iff \ker A_{I(x)}=\{0\}.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Basis Index Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Column bases for full-row-rank standard-form systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have rank \(m\), with \(m\le n\). A basis index set is a subset \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) satisfying \(|B|=m\) and \(\det(A_B)\ne0\), where \(A_B\) is the square submatrix formed by columns indexed by \(B\). Its complementary index set \(N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus B\) is the associated nonbasis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis index set selects exactly m linearly independent columns of a full-row-rank m-by-n constraint matrix; all remaining indices are nonbasic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\text{ is a basis}\iff |B|=m\text{ and }\det(A_B)\ne0.\)

notation.meaning: submatrix formed from columns indexed by B

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduced-Cost Identity, Optimality Test, and Unbounded-Ray Test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For a primal-feasible basis of a standard-form minimization linear program; includes the zero-step degeneracy boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\). Let \(\mathcal B\) be a basis with nonsingular \(B=A_{\mathcal B}\), let \(\mathcal N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\mathcal B\), and suppose \(x_{\mathcal B}=B^{-1}b\geq0\), \(x_{\mathcal N}=0\). Define \(\lambda=B^{-T}c_{\mathcal B}\), \(s_{\mathcal B}=0\), and \(s_{\mathcal N}=c_{\mathcal N}-N^T\lambda\). If \(s_{\mathcal N}\geq0\), then \((x,\lambda,s)\) is optimal. If \(q\in\mathcal N\) has \(s_q<0\), set \(d=B^{-1}A_q\) and \(x_{\mathcal B}(t)=x_{\mathcal B}-dt\), \(x_q(t)=t\). For every feasible \(t\geq0\), \(c^Tx(t)=c^Tx+s_qt\), so the objective decreases strictly when \(t>0\). If \(d\leq0\), the ray is feasible for all \(t\geq0\) and the objective tends to \(-\infty\). Otherwise, \(\theta=\min_{i:d_i>0}(x_{\mathcal B})_i/d_i\) is the largest feasible step and makes at least one basic component zero; \(\theta\) may equal zero in a degenerate pivot.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a primal-feasible basis of a standard-form minimization LP, solving the dual basis equations gives the nonbasic reduced costs. Nonnegative reduced costs certify optimality. If a nonbasic variable has negative reduced cost, increasing it along the associated basis direction changes the objective by its reduced cost times the step and therefore strictly improves the objective for every positive feasible step. If every component of the basis direction is nonpositive, this gives a feasible ray on which the objective tends to minus infinity. Otherwise, the minimum-ratio step is the largest feasible step and makes a basic variable zero; in a degenerate pivot that step can be zero.
assumptions_latex: B=A_{\mathcal B}\text{ is nonsingular},\quad \mathcal N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\mathcal B
\lambda=B^{-T}c_{\mathcal B},\quad s_{\mathcal B}=0,\quad s_{\mathcal N}=c_{\mathcal N}-N^T\lambda
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s_{\mathcal N}\geq0\Rightarrow x\text{ is optimal};\quad s_q<0\Rightarrow c^Tx(t)=c^Tx+s_qt;\quad d\leq0\Rightarrow \inf c^Tx=-\infty;\quad d\not\leq0\Rightarrow \theta=\min_{i:d_i>0}\frac{(x_{\mathcal B})_i}{d_i}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasible Basis and Associated Basic Feasible Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the extract's convention that a basis must induce a feasible standard-form basic solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\). An index set \(\mathcal M\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is a basis in this feasible-basis convention if \(|\mathcal M|=m\), \(B=[A_{\cdot i}]_{i\in\mathcal M}\) is nonsingular, and \(B^{-1}b\ge 0\). Its associated basic feasible point is obtained by setting \(x_i=0\) for \(i\notin\mathcal M\) and is unique; for a suitable permutation matrix \(\Pi\), \(x=\Pi\begin{bmatrix}B^{-1}b\\0\end{bmatrix}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the extract's convention, a basis is a selection of exactly m columns forming a nonsingular matrix and inducing a nonnegative basic solution. Setting every nonbasic variable to zero yields a unique basic feasible point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists!\,x\in P\text{ such that }x_i=0\text{ for }i\notin\mathcal M,\qquad x=\Pi\begin{bmatrix}B^{-1}b\\0\end{bmatrix}.

knowledge_statements.title: Basic Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis-induced solutions of standard-form equality systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have rank \(m\), let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and let \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) be a basis index set with complement \(N\). The basic solution associated with \(B\) is the unique vector \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) determined by \[x_N=0,\qquad x_B=A_B^{-1}b.\] It satisfies \(Ax=b\). For the standard-form feasible region \(P=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^n:Au=b,\ u\ge0\}\), this vector is a basic feasible solution exactly when \(A_B^{-1}b\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis defines a basic solution by setting the nonbasic variables to zero and solving the basis equations; the solution is feasible for the standard-form region exactly when its basic entries are nonnegative.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a basis index set with complement \(N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_N=0,\ x_B=A_B^{-1}b\), and \(x\in P\iff A_B^{-1}b\ge0.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic variables, columns, and basis matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminology and representation associated with a standard-form basic solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let x be a basic solution represented by a basic-index set I=\{B(1),\ldots,B(m)\}. Variables x_i with i\in I are basic and those with i\notin I are nonbasic. The columns A_i for i\in I are the basic columns and form the invertible basis matrix B=A_I. The basic-variable vector satisfies Bx_B=b and therefore x_B=B^{-1}b. Bases are identified by their sets of basic indices, so permuting the same indices does not produce a distinct basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a represented basic solution, the selected variables and columns are basic and the remaining variables are nonbasic. The selected columns form an invertible basis matrix, the basic values equal its inverse times the right-hand side, and reordering the same index set does not create a new basis.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B:=A_I\text{ is invertible},\qquad x_B=B^{-1}b,\qquad I\text{ determines the basis independently of index order}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic, Feasible, and Degenerate Basic Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis-relative definitions for the linear system \(Ax=b\), including feasibility and degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the columns of a selected basis matrix \(B\) be the basic columns of \(A\), and partition the variables into basic and nonbasic components. The vector defined by \(Bx_B=b\) and \(x_N=0\) is the basic solution with respect to \(B\); the components of \(x_B\) are the basic variables. A basic solution is degenerate if at least one basic variable is zero. A vector \(x\) is feasible if \(Ax=b\) and \(x\ge 0\). A feasible basic solution is a basic feasible solution, and a basic feasible solution that is degenerate is a degenerate basic feasible solution. Every basic feasible solution satisfies \(x_B\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a selected basis B, set the nonbasic variables to zero and solve Bx_B=b; the resulting vector is the basic solution, and x_B contains its basic variables. It is degenerate when at least one basic variable is zero. A vector is feasible when it satisfies Ax=b and is nonnegative. A solution that is both basic and feasible is a basic feasible solution; it is a degenerate basic feasible solution when at least one basic variable is zero. Its basic variables are necessarily nonnegative.
assumptions_latex: B\text{ is a selected basis matrix formed from columns of }A
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is the basic solution with respect to }B;\quad x\text{ is feasible if }Ax=b\text{ and }x\ge 0;\quad x\text{ is basic feasible if it is both basic and feasible};\quad x\text{ is degenerate if }(x_B)_i=0\text{ for some }i;\quad x\text{ basic feasible}\Rightarrow x_B\ge 0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic solutions for equality-form LPs with variable bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Also defines free variables and feasibility of a basic solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\max\{cx:Ax=b,\ l\le x\le u\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and bounds may be infinite. A variable \(x_j\) is free or unrestricted if \(l_j=-\infty\) and \(u_j=+\infty\); otherwise it is restricted. A solution \(x^*\) of \(Ax=b\) is basic if the variables can be partitioned into \(m\) basic and \(n-m\) nonbasic variables such that the corresponding \(m\) basic columns form a nonsingular matrix and each restricted nonbasic variable satisfies \(x_j^*=l_j\) or \(x_j^*=u_j\). A basic solution is feasible when \(l\le x^*\le u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basic solution selects m nonsingular basic columns and places every restricted nonbasic variable at one of its bounds. It is feasible when it satisfies all variable bounds. A variable with both bounds infinite is free or unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ is basic exactly when it admits the stated partition, and a basic solution is feasible exactly when }l\le x^*\le u.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Entering variables, leaving variables, and adjacent bases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminology for a single simplex pivot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $B$ and $B'$ be the bases immediately before and after a simplex pivot. A variable that changes from nonbasic in $B$ to basic in $B'$ is the entering variable, and a variable that changes from basic in $B$ to nonbasic in $B'$ is the leaving (or blocking) variable. If $|B\setminus B'|=|B'\setminus B|=1$, then $B$ and $B'$ are adjacent bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a simplex pivot, the variable joining the basis is the entering variable and the variable removed from it is the leaving or blocking variable. Consecutive bases that exchange exactly one basic variable are adjacent bases.
assumptions_latex: $B$ and $B'$ are consecutive bases produced by one simplex pivot.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |B\setminus B'|=|B'\setminus B|=1,\quad\text{so }B\text{ and }B'\text{ are adjacent bases.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminology and selection rule for a primal simplex pivot from a feasible dictionary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a dictionary, the \(x_j\) variables on the left are basic and those on the right are nonbasic; the basic variables constitute the basis. A pivot selects a nonbasic entering variable to improve \(z\), then selects as leaving variable the basic variable whose nonnegativity gives the smallest admissible upper bound on the entering variable's increase. Its equation is the pivot row, and rewriting the dictionary after exchanging the two variables is pivoting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variables on a dictionary's left side are basic, those on its right side are nonbasic, and the basic variables form the basis. A simplex pivot chooses a nonbasic entering variable to improve the objective and a basic leaving variable whose nonnegativity imposes the tightest upper bound on that increase. The leaving variable's equation is the pivot row; constructing the exchanged dictionary is pivoting.
assumptions_latex: \text{The current dictionary represents a feasible solution with all }x_j\ge0.
\text{A nonbasic variable is selected whose increase is intended to improve }z.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The tightest nonnegativity bound determines the leaving variable, and the resulting basis exchange is performed by pivoting.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Implicit bound handling in the simplex method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-variable pivot selection and bound flips for equality-form LPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\max\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ 0\le x\le u\}\), a nonbasic variable is maintained at one of its bounds. If \(x_{\ell_j}^*=0\), it is eligible to enter exactly when its reduced-cost coefficient satisfies \(r_j>0\); if \(x_{\ell_j}^*=u_j<\infty\), it is eligible exactly when \(r_j<0\), moving toward the opposite bound. If the entering variable reaches its opposite bound before a basic variable reaches a bound, it is set to that bound without changing the basis. The same scheme applies to \(\ell\le x\le u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In bounded-variable simplex, each nonbasic variable sits at a bound and may enter only in an improving direction: positive reduced cost from its lower bound or negative reduced cost from its upper bound. If it reaches the opposite bound before any basic variable reaches a bound, its value changes but the basis does not. The rule extends to arbitrary lower and upper bounds.
assumptions_latex: x^*\text{ is a current bounded basic feasible solution, with reduced-cost coefficients }r_j
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{\ell_j}^*=0\Rightarrow(r_j>0\text{ is the entering condition}),\qquad x_{\ell_j}^*=u_j<\infty\Rightarrow(r_j<0\text{ is the entering condition}),\text{ with a bound-to-bound move requiring no basis change if no basic bound is reached first.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every basis \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \(|B|=m\) and nonsingular \(A_B\), define \(x_N(B)=0\) and \(x_B(B)=A_B^{-1}b\), where \(N=B^c\). If the same feasible point is obtained from two distinct bases, then it has fewer than \(m\) positive components and every representing basis has at least one zero basic variable. A nondegenerate basic feasible solution therefore has exactly one representing basis.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-Support Basis Lemma under Nondegeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support-size and feasible-basis consequences for a standard-form polyhedron with full row rank and only nondegenerate basic feasible solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n:A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},\ \mathbf{x}\geq 0\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\), and suppose every basic feasible solution of \(P\) is nondegenerate. For \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}\in P\), let \(N=\{i:\bar{x}_i>0\}\). Then there exists \(B\subseteq N\) with \(|B|=m\) such that the columns of \(A_B\) are linearly independent and the corresponding basic solution is feasible. Consequently, \(|N|\geq m\). If \(|N|=m\), then \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}\) is a basic feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under full row rank and nondegeneracy of every basic feasible solution, the positive support of any feasible point contains a feasible basis and has at least m indices. If it has exactly m indices, the point is itself basic feasible.
assumptions_latex: \text{Every basic feasible solution of }P\text{ is nondegenerate}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\exists B\subseteq N:\ |B|=m,\ \operatorname{rank}(A_B)=m,\text{ and the }B\text{-basic solution is feasible}\right]\land |N|\geq m\land\left(|N|=m\implies\bar{\mathbf{x}}\text{ is a basic feasible solution}\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One Iteration of the Primal Revised Simplex Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard-form minimization iteration from a basic feasible solution; includes optimality and unboundedness termination tests and basis-inverse updating.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) with a nonsingular basis matrix \(B=[A_{B(1)},\ldots,A_{B(m)}]\), an associated basic feasible solution \(x\), and \(B^{-1}\). Compute \(p^\top=c_{\mathcal B}^\top B^{-1}\) and \(\bar c_j=c_j-p^\top A_j\). If every \(\bar c_j\ge0\), terminate with \(x\) optimal. Otherwise choose \(j\) with \(\bar c_j<0\) and set \(u=B^{-1}A_j\). If \(u_i\le0\) for all \(i\), terminate with optimal value \(-\infty\). Otherwise set \(\theta^*=\min_{i:u_i>0}x_{B(i)}/u_i\), choose \(\ell\) attaining the minimum, and replace \(A_{B(\ell)}\) by \(A_j\). The new basic feasible solution satisfies \(y_j=\theta^*\) and \(y_{B(i)}=x_{B(i)}-\theta^*u_i\) for \(i\ne\ell\). To obtain the new inverse \(\bar B^{-1}\), apply row operations to \([B^{-1}\mid u]\) so that its last column becomes \(e_\ell\); its first \(m\) columns then equal \(\bar B^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a basis, its inverse, and the associated basic feasible solution, compute simplex multipliers and reduced costs. Nonnegative reduced costs certify optimality. Otherwise choose a negative-reduced-cost entering column and compute its transformed column. If that column has no positive component, the problem is unbounded below. Otherwise use the minimum-ratio test to select the leaving column, update the basic variables, exchange the basis columns, and recover the new basis inverse by row-reducing the augmented matrix formed from the old inverse and transformed entering column.
assumptions_latex: \min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\text{ is in primal standard form.}
x\text{ is the basic feasible solution associated with }B.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar c\ge0\Rightarrow x\text{ is optimal};\qquad \bar c_j<0\ \land\ B^{-1}A_j\le0\Rightarrow \inf c^\top x=-\infty;\qquad\text{otherwise the ratio-test pivot produces a new basic feasible solution and }\bar B^{-1}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduced-Cost Improvement and Unboundedness Alternative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For a nondegenerate basic feasible solution of a minimization LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^0\) be a nondegenerate basic feasible solution with objective value \(z_0\), and let \(c_j-z_j\) denote the reduced cost of column \(\mathbf a_j\). If \(c_j-z_j<0\) for some \(j\), then there exists a feasible solution \(x\) with objective value \(z<z_0\). If \(\mathbf a_j\) can replace a column of the original basis and yield a new basic feasible solution, that new solution has objective value strictly below \(z_0\). If no such substitution can yield a basic feasible solution, then the feasible set \(K\) is unbounded and \(\inf_{x\in K} c^{\mathsf T}x=-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a nondegenerate basic feasible solution of a minimization LP, a negative reduced cost guarantees a feasible solution with strictly lower objective value. If the associated column can enter the basis, the resulting basic feasible solution is strictly better; if it cannot yield a new basic feasible solution, the feasible set is unbounded and the objective is unbounded below.
assumptions_latex: x^0\text{ is a nondegenerate basic feasible solution}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x\in K\colon c^{\mathsf T}x<z_0,\quad\text{with the stated pivot-or-unboundedness alternative}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimal Feasible and Optimal Basic Feasible Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For a linear program in standard form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{\mathbf c^T\mathbf x:\mathbf A\mathbf x=\mathbf b,\ \mathbf x\geq\mathbf0\}\), a feasible vector \(\mathbf x^*\) is an optimal feasible solution if \(\mathbf c^T\mathbf x^*\leq\mathbf c^T\mathbf x\) for every feasible \(\mathbf x\). If such an optimal feasible solution is basic, it is an optimal basic feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible solution of a standard-form linear program is optimal if it attains the minimum objective value over all feasible solutions. An optimal feasible solution that is basic is an optimal basic feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Bigl[\forall\mathbf x\,\bigl((\mathbf A\mathbf x=\mathbf b\land\mathbf x\geq\mathbf0)\Rightarrow\mathbf c^T\mathbf x^*\leq\mathbf c^T\mathbf x\bigr)\Bigr]\Rightarrow \mathbf x^*\text{ is an optimal feasible solution};\quad \bigl(\mathbf x^*\text{ is optimal feasible}\land\mathbf x^*\text{ is basic}\bigr)\Rightarrow\mathbf x^*\text{ is an optimal basic feasible solution}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Phase-I certificate for inadmissible transportation cells
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to a transportation system with nonnegative flows, adjusted row and column totals, and a designated set of cells constrained to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A fixed value \(x_{pq}=\alpha\) may be eliminated by subtracting \(\alpha\) from the corresponding row and column totals and imposing zero on its residual variable. For a set \(I\) of inadmissible cells, let \(d_{ij}=1\) for \((i,j)\in I\) and \(d_{ij}=0\) otherwise, and solve \[w^*=\min_{x\in T}\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n d_{ij}x_{ij},\] where \(T\) is the nonempty transportation-feasible set after the adjustments. Then the transportation problem satisfying \(x_{ij}=0\) for every \((i,j)\in I\) is feasible if and only if \(w^*=0\); if \(w^*>0\), it is infeasible. When \(w^*=0\), any inadmissible variable remaining basic is zero. A nonbasic inadmissible variable with \(d_{ij}-u_i-v_j>0\) at the end of Phase I may be excluded from Phase II.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminate a fixed transportation flow by reducing its row and column totals by the fixed amount and fixing the residual flow at zero. To test whether all forbidden cells can be zero, minimize the total flow through them over the adjusted transportation constraints. The restricted problem is feasible exactly when this minimum is zero, and a positive minimum certifies infeasibility. Forbidden variables that remain basic at a zero Phase-I optimum have value zero; a nonbasic forbidden variable with positive relative infeasibility may be removed before Phase II.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\cap\{x:x_{ij}=0\ \forall(i,j)\in I\}\ne\varnothing\iff w^*=0;\qquad w^*>0\implies\text{the restricted transportation problem is infeasible}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tableau Primal Simplex Algorithm and Nondegenerate Termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For a minimization-form linear program, starting from a tableau representing a basic feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting from a tableau for a basic feasible solution, compute the reduced costs \(r_j\). If \(r_j\ge 0\) for every nonbasic variable, stop with an optimal basic feasible solution. Otherwise choose \(q\) with \(r_q<0\). If \(\bar a_{iq}\le 0\) for every \(i\), stop because the problem is unbounded. Otherwise choose \(p\in\arg\min_{i:\,\bar a_{iq}>0}\bar a_{i0}/\bar a_{iq}\), pivot on entry \((p,q)\), update the tableau, and repeat. If all encountered basic feasible solutions are nondegenerate, each nonterminal pivot strictly decreases the objective, no basis repeats, and the method terminates finitely with either an optimal basic feasible solution or a certificate of unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Begin with a tableau for a basic feasible solution. Stop as optimal when all reduced costs are nonnegative. Otherwise select a variable with negative reduced cost. If its pivot column has no positive entry, declare the problem unbounded; if it does, use the minimum-ratio test to select the leaving variable, pivot, and repeat. Under nondegeneracy, every nonterminal pivot strictly decreases the objective, so finite termination occurs at optimality or unboundedness.
assumptions_latex: \text{The linear program is in the minimization tableau convention.}
\text{An initial basic feasible solution and its tableau are available.}
\text{For the finite-termination guarantee, all encountered basic feasible solutions are nondegenerate.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The iterations terminate finitely at an optimal basic feasible solution or establish unboundedness.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basis Representation and Degenerate Basis Multiplicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The converse from a basis to an extreme point is understood for a basis whose induced basic solution is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every extreme point (equivalently, basic feasible solution) has at least one representing basis, possibly more than one, and every feasible basis determines a unique extreme point. If an extreme point has multiple representing bases, it is degenerate. Conversely, for a degenerate extreme point and an associated basis, multiple representing bases exist if and only if Ax=b does not force the corresponding degenerate basic variables to be identically zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every extreme point has a representing basis, while a feasible basis determines one extreme point. Multiple bases for the same extreme point imply degeneracy; for a degenerate extreme point, multiplicity occurs exactly when the equality system does not structurally force the associated zero basic variables to remain zero.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduced-cost descent with finite and infinite lower-bound cases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical minimization-simplex sign convention in which positive \(z_j-c_j\) indicates improvement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \text{Let }x^{(0)}\text{ be the current feasible solution with objective }z_0.\text{ If, for some fixed }j,\ z_j-c_j>0,\text{ then feasible solutions }x\text{ exist with }z(x)<z_0.\text{ If }\inf_{x\in\mathcal F}z(x)>-\infty,\text{ an improving feasible solution with exactly }m\text{ positive variables can be constructed. If }\inf_{x\in\mathcal F}z(x)=-\infty,\text{ feasible solutions with exactly }m+1\text{ positive variables can be constructed with arbitrarily small objective value.}
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a fixed reduced-cost expression satisfies z_j-c_j>0, feasible solutions improving on the current objective value z_0 can be constructed. When the objective has a finite lower bound, an improving feasible solution with exactly m positive variables can be constructed. When the lower bound is negative infinity, feasible solutions with exactly m+1 positive variables can have arbitrarily small objective value.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic, Basic Feasible, Nondegenerate, and Degenerate Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard-form equality systems with nonnegative variables.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniqueness for a Fixed Basis and Basis Multiplicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States that a fixed nonsingular basis determines at most one feasible solution while preserving the converse failure boundary: one basic feasible solution may correspond to several bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) satisfy \(|B|=m\) and \(A_B\) nonsingular. knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(A=(1\;0)\), \(b=0\), and \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^2:x_1=0,\ x\ge0\}\). At the vertex \(v=(0,0)\), the basis \(B=\{1\}\) is feasible and degenerate because \(x_1=0\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vertex \(v\) and an edge \(E\) of \(P\) are incident when \(v\in E\). If \(E\) is bounded, then there are unique distinct vertices \(u,v\) such that \(E=[u,v]\), and these are exactly the vertices incident to \(E\). If \(E\) is unbounded and contains a vertex, then there exist a unique incident vertex \(v\) and a nonzero extreme recession direction \(r\), unique up to positive scaling, such that \(E=\{v+tr:t\ge0\}\). Consequently, a bounded edge has two vertex incidences, while an unbounded edge has one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incidence means membership. A bounded edge has exactly two endpoint vertices, while an unbounded edge containing a vertex has one endpoint and one extreme recession direction.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\), and let \(x\) be a degenerate basic feasible solution. Degeneracy permits distinct feasible bases \(B_1\ne B_2\) to determine the same point \(x\). Consequently, a pivot between adjacent bases can have zero step length and leave the geometric vertex unchanged. Conversely, when two distinct vertices are joined by an edge, degeneracy can allow several choices of leaving or entering indices, hence several basis pivots, to represent that same geometric transition. Thus adjacency in the graph of feasible bases is generally neither an injective representation of vertex adjacency nor a one-to-one representation of edge incidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a degenerate vertex, different adjacent bases may represent the same point, while a single geometric edge transition may have several pivot representations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normalized recession directions and extreme directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized cross-section of the recession cone for a canonical nonnegative polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}\), the nonzero recession directions are exactly the vectors \(d\ne0\) satisfying \(Ad\le0\) and \(d\ge0\). Because such vectors are nonnegative, each recession ray has a unique representative satisfying \(\|d\|_1=\mathbf1^\top d=1\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession Cone of a Polyhedron
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the recession cone and gives its inequality and standard-form representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\geq b\}\neq\varnothing\) and \(y\in P\). Then \[\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:A(y+\lambda d)\geq b\text{ for every }\lambda\geq0\}=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ad\geq0\}.\] Thus \(\operatorname{rec}(P)\) is a polyhedral cone independent of \(y\), and its nonzero elements are the rays of \(P\). If \(P=\{x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\neq\varnothing\), then \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d:Ad=0,\ d\geq0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty polyhedron Ax ≥ b, the recession directions are exactly the vectors d satisfying Ad ≥ 0, independently of the chosen feasible starting point. In standard form they are the nonnegative null vectors of A.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d:A(y+\lambda d)\geq b\ \forall\lambda\geq0\}=\{d:Ad\geq0\},\qquad P=\{x:Ax=b,x\geq0\}\Rightarrow\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d:Ad=0,d\geq0\}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes objective unboundedness below on a pointed polyhedral cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\geq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) be a pointed polyhedral cone. Then \[\inf_{x\in C}c^{\mathsf T}x=-\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{some extreme ray }d\text{ of }C\text{ satisfies }c^{\mathsf T}d<0.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme Rays and Complete Representative Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the source's active-constraint definition of extreme rays and records scaling equivalence and finiteness for polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Relative to a defining inequality system for a polyhedral cone \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), a nonzero \(x\in C\) is called an extreme ray when \(n-1\) linearly independent constraints are active at \(x\). An extreme ray of \(\operatorname{rec}(P)\), for a nonempty polyhedron \(P\), is also called an extreme ray of \(P\). Two extreme rays are equivalent when one is a positive multiple of the other. A polyhedron has finitely many such equivalence classes, and a complete set of extreme rays contains exactly one representative from each class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a fixed inequality description, a nonzero cone element is an extreme ray when n−1 linearly independent constraints are active there. Extreme rays of a polyhedron are those of its recession cone. Positive multiples are equivalent, only finitely many equivalence classes occur, and a complete set selects one representative from each class.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme directions and extreme rays
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extremality among recession directions, with directions identified up to positive scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty convex set. Two nonzero directions \(d_1,d_2\) are equivalent if \(d_1=\alpha d_2\) for some \(\alpha>0\). A recession direction \(d\) of \(C\) is extreme if it cannot be represented as \(d=\lambda_1d_1+\lambda_2d_2\), where \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2>0\) and \(d_1,d_2\) are nonequivalent recession directions of \(C\). A ray contained in \(C\) whose direction is extreme is an extreme ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directions differing only by positive scaling are equivalent. An extreme direction cannot be expressed as a positive combination of two inequivalent recession directions, and a ray contained in the set with such a direction is an extreme ray.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d\text{ is extreme}\iff \nexists\,d_1,d_2,\lambda_1,\lambda_2\text{ with }d_1\not\sim d_2,\ \lambda_1,\lambda_2>0,\ d=\lambda_1d_1+\lambda_2d_2;\quad \{x_0+\lambda d:\lambda\ge0\}\subseteq C\text{ is an extreme ray when }d\text{ is extreme}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\operatorname{rec}(P)\) for a nonempty polyhedron \(P\). Its lineality space is \[\operatorname{lin}(K)=K\cap(-K).\] The lineality regime occurs when \(\operatorname{lin}(K)\ne\{0\}\). Equivalently, some \(d\ne0\) satisfies both \(d\in\operatorname{rec}(P)\) and \(-d\in\operatorname{rec}(P)\), so for every \(x\in P\), \[x+td\in P\qquad\text{for all }t\in\mathbb{R}.\] Hence \(P\) contains an affine line; conversely, any affine line contained in \(P\) supplies a nonzero lineality direction.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\operatorname{rec}(P)\) be a nonzero pointed polyhedral cone. Then \(K\) has finitely many extreme rays \(R_1,\ldots,R_q\). Choosing any generator \(r_j\in R_j\setminus\{0\}\) for each ray yields the representation \[K=\operatorname{cone}\{r_1,\ldots,r_q\}=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^q\lambda_jr_j:\lambda_j\ge0\right\}.\] Moreover, every conic generating set for \(K\) must contain a vector on each \(R_j\). Thus the extreme rays give the irredundant directional types of the pointed recession cone, up to positive rescaling of their generators.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral cone by homogeneous inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Halfspace and homogeneous-inequality characterization of polyhedral cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a polyhedral cone if it is the intersection of finitely many halfspaces whose boundary hyperplanes pass through the origin. Equivalently, for some \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le 0\}\). The \(i\)-th row of \(A\) is normal to the boundary hyperplane of the \(i\)-th halfspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral cone is an intersection of finitely many halfspaces whose boundary hyperplanes contain the origin. Equivalently, it is the solution set of finitely many homogeneous linear inequalities, with each matrix row normal to the corresponding boundary hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x:(a^i)^\top x\le 0\}=\{x:Ax\le 0\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\geq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\). The following are equivalent: (i) \(0\) is an extreme point of \(C\); (ii) \(C\) contains no line; (iii) among \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\) there are \(n\) linearly independent vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a homogeneous inequality-defined polyhedral cone, the origin is an extreme point exactly when the cone contains no line, equivalently when the defining normals span R^n.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in\operatorname{ext}(C)\iff C\text{ contains no line}\iff \operatorname{rank}[a_1\ \cdots\ a_m]=n

children.title: Nonpointed Cones
children.top_down_role: Cones containing nontrivial linear subspaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonpointed Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonpointedness for convex cones in finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex cone \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonpointed precisely when it contains a nonzero linear subspace. Equivalently, there exists \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) such that \(d\in C\) and \(-d\in C\), or, equivalently, the line \(\{\lambda d:\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\}\) is contained in \(C\). Thus nonpointedness is exactly the condition \(C\cap(-C)\ne\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex cone is nonpointed exactly when it contains a line through the origin, equivalently when it contains some nonzero direction and its negative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is nonpointed}\iff C\cap(-C)\ne\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: set of negatives of elements of the cone

children.title: Cone Lineality Boundary
children.top_down_role: Separation of pointedness regimes through the cone lineality space.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone Lineality Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The lineality-space criterion separating pointed and nonpointed cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex cone \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), define its lineality space by \(L(C)=C\cap(-C)\). This set is the largest linear subspace contained in \(C\). The pointedness boundary is characterized by \(L(C)=\{0\}\): the cone is pointed exactly in this case, while \(\dim L(C)>0\) characterizes the nonpointed regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lineality space is the largest subspace inside a cone. Its dimension is zero for pointed cones and positive for nonpointed cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is pointed}\iff L(C)=\{0\};\quad C\text{ is nonpointed}\iff\dim L(C)>0.\)

children.title: Pointed Quotient Structure
children.top_down_role: Lineality removal leading to a pointed quotient representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Pointed Quotient Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointed reduction obtained by quotienting a cone by its lineality space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a convex cone, let \(L=C\cap(-C)\), and let \(\pi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n/L\) be the quotient map. Then \(\pi(C)\) is a pointed convex cone. Moreover, \(C=\pi^{-1}(\pi(C))\), and if \(C\) is polyhedral, then \(\pi(C)\) is polyhedral in the quotient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quotienting a convex cone by its lineality space produces a pointed convex cone, the original cone is exactly the inverse image of its quotient image, and polyhedrality is preserved.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi(C)\text{ is pointed},\quad C=\pi^{-1}(\pi(C));\quad C\text{ polyhedral}\Rightarrow\pi(C)\text{ polyhedral}.\)

notation.meaning: canonical quotient map onto the space modulo lineality

knowledge_statements.title: Finitely Generated Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generator representation of cones in finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cone \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is finitely generated if there exist vectors \(v^1,\ldots,v^k\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \[C=\operatorname{cone}\{v^1,\ldots,v^k\}=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i v^i:\lambda_i\ge 0\text{ for every }i\right\}.\] The vectors are conic generators; the representation need not be irredundant or unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finitely generated cone consists of all nonnegative linear combinations of a finite list of vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\operatorname{cone}\{v^1,\ldots,v^k\}.\)

notation.meaning: set of all finite nonnegative combinations of vectors in the finite set V

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finitely generated sets are polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converse polyhedrality result for finite point-and-direction representations, including finite convex hulls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If
\[
Q=\operatorname{conv}\{x^1,\ldots,x^k\}+\operatorname{cone}\{w^1,\ldots,w^r\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n,
\]
then \(Q\) is a polyhedron. In particular, for any finite family \(x^1,\ldots,x^k\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(\operatorname{conv}\{x^1,\ldots,x^k\}\) is a bounded polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every set generated by finitely many point generators and direction generators is a polyhedron; in particular, the convex hull of finitely many vectors is a bounded polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q\text{ is a polyhedron};\quad \operatorname{conv}\{x^1,\ldots,x^k\}\text{ is a bounded polyhedron}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence and uniqueness of a nearest point in a finitely generated cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean nearest-point property for finitely generated convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C=\operatorname{cone}(\mathbf a_1,\ldots,\mathbf a_n)\subseteq\mathbb R^m and let \mathbf b\in\mathbb R^m\setminus C. Then there exists a unique \mathbf z\in C such that \|\mathbf b-\mathbf z\|=\min_{\mathbf x\in C}\|\mathbf b-\mathbf x\|.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists!\,\mathbf z\in C:\ \|\mathbf b-\mathbf z\|=\min_{\mathbf x\in C}\|\mathbf b-\mathbf x\|

children.title: Cone Faces
children.top_down_role: Facial structure within polyhedral cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Faces of convex cones, including improper faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a convex cone and let \(F\subseteq C\). Under the convention that the empty set is an improper face, \(F\) is a face of \(C\) if either \(F=\varnothing\), or \(F\) is a convex cone such that, for all \(x,y\in C\), \(x+y\in F\) implies \(x,y\in F\). For nonempty \(F\), this is equivalent to requiring that whenever a relative-interior point of a segment contained in \(C\) belongs to \(F\), both endpoints belong to \(F\). The sets \(C\) and \(\varnothing\) are the improper faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated convention, the empty set and the cone itself are improper faces. Every nonempty face is a convex subcone that contains both summands whenever it contains their sum; equivalently, it contains the endpoints of any cone segment whose relative interior meets the face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\unlhd C\iff F=\varnothing\text{ or }[F\text{ is a convex cone and }\forall x,y\in C,\ x+y\in F\Rightarrow x,y\in F].\)

notation.meaning: F is a face of C

children.title: Extreme Rays
children.top_down_role: One-dimensional extremal generators of pointed cone structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme Rays
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme rays of pointed or nonpointed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a convex cone and let \(r\in C\setminus\{0\}\). The ray \(R=\{\lambda r:\lambda\ge0\}\) is an extreme ray of \(C\) if \(R\) is a face of \(C\). Equivalently, for all \(x,y\in C\), the relation \(x+y\in R\) implies \(x,y\in R\). Consequently, a cone containing nonzero lineality has no extreme rays under this facial definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A ray is extreme when any decomposition in the cone of a point on that ray uses only vectors on the same ray. Under this facial definition, a cone with nonzero lineality has no extreme rays.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R=\mathbb{R}_+r\text{ is extreme}\iff[\forall x,y\in C,\ x+y\in R\Rightarrow x,y\in R].\)

source_refs.locator: 4.8. Cones and extreme rays p. 174

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Resolution theorem for polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite vertex-and-ray representation of a nonempty polyhedron having an extreme point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\ge b\}\) be nonempty and have at least one extreme point. If \(x^1,\ldots,x^k\) are all extreme points of \(P\) and \(w^1,\ldots,w^r\) form a complete set of its extreme rays, then
\[
P=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i x^i+\sum_{j=1}^r\theta_j w^j:\lambda_i\ge0,\ \theta_j\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point of a nonempty polyhedron having an extreme point is a convex combination of its extreme points plus a nonnegative combination of its extreme rays, and every such combination belongs to the polyhedron.
assumptions_latex: P\text{ has at least one extreme point}
\{w^1,\ldots,w^r\}\text{ is a complete set of extreme rays of }P
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P=\operatorname{conv}\{x^1,\ldots,x^k\}+\operatorname{cone}\{w^1,\ldots,w^r\}

children.title: Extreme Line Generators
children.top_down_role: Generator structure associated with lineality in nonpointed cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme Line Generators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Line generators used to represent the lineality of a polyhedral cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a polyhedral cone with lineality space \(L=C\cap(-C)\). Choose a basis \(\ell^1,\ldots,\ell^q\) of \(L\). Then every \(z\in L\) has the unique representation \(z=\sum_{j=1}^q\mu_j\ell^j\) with \(\mu_j\in\mathbb{R}\), and \[L=\operatorname{cone}\{\ell^1,-\ell^1,\ldots,\ell^q,-\ell^q\}.\] These basis vectors are line generators; unlike extreme rays, they are not canonically determined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis of a cone's lineality space gives free-sign line generators, equivalently paired positive and negative conic generators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\cap(-C)=\operatorname{span}\{\ell^1,\ldots,\ell^q\}=\operatorname{cone}\{\pm\ell^1,\ldots,\pm\ell^q\}.\)

children.title: Face–Generator Incidence
children.top_down_role: Containment relations linking cone faces to extremal generators.

knowledge_statements.title: Face–Generator Incidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generator membership characterizes nonempty faces of finitely generated cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\operatorname{cone}\{v^1,\ldots,v^k\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(F\) be a nonempty face of \(C\). Then \[F=\operatorname{cone}\{v^i:v^i\in F\},\] where \(\operatorname{cone}\varnothing=\{0\}\). More precisely, if \(x\in F\) admits a representation \(x=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i v^i\) with \(\lambda_i\ge0\), then every generator satisfying \(\lambda_i>0\) belongs to \(F\). Thus every nonempty face is generated by the original generators incident with it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty face of a finitely generated cone is generated exactly by the listed generators lying in that face, with the conic hull of the empty family understood as the zero cone. Every positively used generator in a representation of a face point must belong to that face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\operatorname{cone}\{v^i:v^i\in F\}.\)

notation.meaning: a member of the chosen finite generator family
the zero cone under the convention used in this record

children.title: Dual-Cone Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric roles of dual cones in polyhedral analysis.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Cone Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative-inner-product convention for dual cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a cone \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its dual cone is \[C^*=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\text{ for every }x\in C\}.\] The set \(C^*\) is always a closed convex cone. If \(C\) is a closed convex cone, then \(C^{**}=C\). Furthermore, inclusion reverses under duality: \(C_1\subseteq C_2\) implies \(C_2^*\subseteq C_1^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual cone contains vectors having nonnegative inner product with every primal cone vector; it is closed and convex, reverses inclusion, and satisfies bipolarity for closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^*\text{ is closed and convex};\quad C\text{ closed convex}\Rightarrow C^{**}=C.\)

notation.meaning: dual cone under the nonnegative pairing convention

children.title: Polar-Cone Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric roles of polar cones in polyhedral analysis.

knowledge_statements.title: Polar-Cone Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonpositive-inner-product convention for polar cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its polar cone is \[C^\circ=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle y,x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }x\in C\}.\] The set \(C^\circ\) is a closed convex cone. For nonempty sets \(C_1,C_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), inclusion reverses under polarity: \(C_1\subseteq C_2\) implies \(C_2^\circ\subseteq C_1^\circ\). Moreover, \(C^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cone}C)\); hence if \(C\) is a closed convex cone, then \(C^{\circ\circ}=C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar cone contains vectors having nonpositive inner product with every vector in the original set. It is a closed convex cone, reverses inclusion, and its bipolar is the closure of the conic hull; consequently a closed convex cone equals its bipolar.
assumptions_latex: \(C_1,C_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) are nonempty when inclusion reversal is invoked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cone}C);\quad C\text{ closed convex cone}\Rightarrow C^{\circ\circ}=C.\)

notation.meaning: polar cone under the nonpositive pairing convention

children.title: Dual–Polar Convention Mapping
children.top_down_role: Sign conventions, ambient spaces, plus translation between dual-cone terminology and polar-cone terminology.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual–Polar Convention Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign conversion between dual- and polar-cone conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Adopt the conventions \(C^*=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\text{ for every }x\in C\}\) and \(C^\circ=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }x\in C\}\). Then \[C^\circ=-C^*\qquad\text{and}\qquad C^*=-C^\circ.\] Hence any assertion expressed with one convention converts to the other by negating the dual variable; no geometric information is changed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With nonnegative dual and nonpositive polar conventions, the polar cone is the negative of the dual cone, so formulas translate by negating the dual variable.
assumptions_latex: Dual and polar cones use the displayed sign conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^\circ=-C^*\) and \(C^*=-C^\circ\).

children.title: Halfspace Inequality Descriptions
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral descriptions expressed through halfspace inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Halfspace Inequality Descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite closed-halfspace representation of polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) has a finite halfspace inequality description if there exist \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\) such that \[P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\}.\] Such sets are precisely polyhedra. The description may contain redundant inequalities and is generally nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedron is exactly the intersection of finitely many closed affine halfspaces, equivalently the solution set of finitely many linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\text{ is a polyhedron}\iff P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\text{ for some finite }m,A,b.\)

notation.meaning: i-th row of the inequality matrix

children.title: Affine Equality Descriptions
children.top_down_role: Affine restrictions represented through equality constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Equality Descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional equality-form description of an affine set, including the inconsistent case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), the affine equality description is \[P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b\}.\] If the system is consistent and \(x^0\in P\), then \[P=x^0+\ker A=\{x^0+z:z\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ Az=0\}.\] If it is inconsistent, then \(P=\varnothing\). Thus every nonempty equality-described set is an affine translate of a linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solutions of linear equalities form either the empty set or a translate of the null space of the coefficient matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\varnothing\) or \(P=x^0+\ker A\) for any \(x^0\in P\).

notation.meaning: Any feasible point of the equality system.

children.title: Mixed Constraint Descriptions
children.top_down_role: Representations combining halfspace inequalities with affine equalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Constraint Descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite systems combining weak linear inequalities and affine equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \(C\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times n}\), and \(d\in\mathbb{R}^p\), a mixed constraint description has the form \[P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b,\ Cx=d\},\] where \(Ax\le b\) is interpreted componentwise. Such a set is a polyhedron, possibly empty, because each equality can equivalently be replaced by the two inequalities \(Cx\le d\) and \(-Cx\le-d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed description intersects finitely many closed halfspaces with an affine equality set and therefore defines a possibly empty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\{x:Ax\le b,\ Cx=d\}\) is a polyhedron.

children.title: Point Generators
children.top_down_role: Point-based components of finite polyhedral generator descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Point Generators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite point generators and their convex combinations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite family \(V=\{v^1,\ldots,v^k\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its point-generated set is the convex hull \[\operatorname{conv}(V)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i v^i:\lambda_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1\right\}.\] The members of \(V\) are point generators. A set \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is generated by \(V\) alone precisely when \(Q=\operatorname{conv}(V)\); such a set is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Point generators produce all convex combinations of a finite set; the resulting set is a bounded polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q=\operatorname{conv}(V)\) consists exactly of the displayed convex combinations.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative convex-combination weights summing to one.

children.title: Recession-Ray Generators
children.top_down_role: Ray-based components capturing unbounded polyhedral directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession-Ray Generators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite generators for the recession cone of a nonempty convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty convex set \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its recession cone is \[\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{r\in\mathbb{R}^n:x+\alpha r\in P\ \text{for every }x\in P,\ \alpha\ge0\}.\] A finite family \(R=\{r^1,\ldots,r^q\}\) is a recession-ray generator family when \[\operatorname{rec}(P)=\operatorname{cone}(R)=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^q\mu_jr^j:\mu_j\ge0\right\}.\] Nonzero members of \(R\) determine recession rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recession-ray generators conically generate every direction along which a nonempty convex set remains feasible indefinitely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) generates the recession directions exactly when \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\operatorname{cone}(R)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Point–Ray Descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite convex-plus-conic generator descriptions of polyhedra without explicit line generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite nonempty \(V=\{v^1,\ldots,v^k\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and finite \(R=\{r^1,\ldots,r^q\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), the mixed point–ray description is \[P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i v^i+\sum_{j=1}^q\mu_jr^j:\lambda_i,\mu_j\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1\right\}.\] Every displayed point belongs to a translate of the cone generated by \(R\), with its base in \(\operatorname{conv}(V)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed generator description adds a conic combination of recession directions to a convex combination of base points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Independent feasible columns yield an extreme point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient condition for extremality in a nonnegative equality-form polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_1,\ldots,P_n\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(K=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^n:\sum_{j=1}^n x_jP_j=P_0\}\). If \(k\le m\), the vectors \(P_1,\ldots,P_k\) are linearly independent, and \(x_i\ge0\) satisfy \(\sum_{i=1}^k x_iP_i=P_0\), then \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_k,0,\ldots,0)\) is an extreme point of K.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible standard-form point supported on at most m linearly independent columns is an extreme point of the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x_1,\ldots,x_k,0,\ldots,0)\in\operatorname{ext}(K)

knowledge_statements.title: Lineality-Aware Generator Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generator syntax separating bounded, one-sided recession, and two-sided lineality components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A lineality-aware finite generator representation of a nonempty polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) has the form \[P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)+\operatorname{span}(D),\] equivalently \[x=\sum_i\lambda_i v^i+\sum_j\mu_jr^j+\sum_\ell\nu_\ell d^\ell,\qquad \lambda_i,\mu_j\ge0,\quad\sum_i\lambda_i=1,\quad\nu_\ell\in\mathbb{R}.\] The span term represents reversible directions and may be chosen equal to the lineality space \(\operatorname{lin}(P)=\operatorname{rec}(P)\cap-\operatorname{rec}(P)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This representation separates convex base points, one-sided recession rays, and freely signed generators of the polyhedron’s lineality space.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite and nonempty; \(R\) and \(D\) are finite
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)+\operatorname{span}(D)\), with \(\operatorname{span}(D)=\operatorname{lin}(P)\) when lineality is represented exactly.

notation.meaning: Largest linear subspace contained in the recession cone of P.
Unrestricted coefficient of a lineality generator.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Polytope Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional bounded case of the Minkowski–Weyl theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty. Then \(P\) is a bounded polyhedron if and only if there exists a finite nonempty set \(V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \[P=\operatorname{conv}(V).\] Moreover, when \(P\) is a bounded polyhedron, \(V\) may be chosen as the finite set \(\operatorname{vert}(P)\) of all vertices of \(P\), giving \(P=\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{vert}(P))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty set is a bounded polyhedron exactly when it is the convex hull of finitely many points; its vertices suffice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is a bounded polyhedron if and only if \(P=\operatorname{conv}(V)\) for some finite nonempty \(V\).
